query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A rapid, tailored annealing‐quench cycle applied to as‐cast eutectic high‐entropy alloys will refine the natural lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, thereby simultaneously increasing both yield strength and ductility compared to conventional processing.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast eutectic high‐entropy alloy with a relatively coarse and non-uniform lamellar fcc/B2 structure.
generation.intervention: A single, precisely controlled rapid annealing-quench cycle designed to refine lamellar spacing and adjust phase morphology.
generation.conditions: Ambient and moderately elevated temperatures under standard quasi-static mechanical testing conditions typical of structural applications.
generation.structural_mediator: A more uniform and finely spaced lamellar microstructure that enhances phase boundary distribution.
generation.mechanism: The refined lamellar spacing increases phase boundary strengthening by hindering dislocation motion (thereby raising strength) while preserving or even enhancing the connectivity of the softer fcc phase, which facilitates dislocation mobility to improve ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is expected to show measurable improvements in both yield strength and ductility relative to the baseline as‐cast or conventionally heat-treated alloy. Although the precise percentage improvements are uncertain without optimization, the integrated microstructural refinement should mitigate the conventional strength–ductility trade-off.
generation.baseline: The standard as-cast (or conventionally heat-treated) EHEA that exhibits a coarser lamellar structure with either high strength and limited ductility or vice versa.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective under quasi-static loading at temperatures relevant for structural applications; its benefits may diminish at very high strain rates or under thermal conditions far outside the annealing-quench regime. Moreover, if the annealing temperature or quench rate deviates from the optimal window, the desired microstructural refinement may not be achieved.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of strength and ductility improvements is uncertain and likely depends on fine-tuning the thermal cycle parameters; also, the optimal processing window for different alloy compositions may vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same batch of as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy. Apply the tailored rapid annealing-quench cycle to one set while maintaining standard processing conditions for the control set. Subject both sets to identical quasi-static mechanical tensile tests under ambient and moderately elevated temperatures. Use high-resolution microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM/TEM) to confirm lamellar spacing differences between the two groups.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapid annealing-quench treatment does not yield statistically significant simultaneous enhancements in both yield strength and ductility (relative to the control samples) and no corresponding refinement of lamellar spacing is observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. decision.trend: Early work on eutectic HEAs (as exemplified by PMC4145285) established that designing a self‐assembled lamellar (fcc/B2) microstructure could yield a good balance between strength and ductility. Subsequent processing steps, like cold rolling, boosted strength further; however, these improvements came with a reduction in ductility. The incremental exploration of processing routes has typically been aimed at tuning phase fractions or refining the microstructure, but they have not overcome the intrinsic trade‐off in a single integrated intervention.
decision.unsolved: The unresolved challenge is to identify a single processing modification that tailors the eutectic microstructure so as to simultaneously elevate both strength and ductility, without resorting to separate sequential steps that individually target one property at the expense of the other.
decision.lever: A tailored rapid annealing-quench cycle designed to refine the natural lamellar spacing and adjust phase morphology
decision.why: Building on the trend of processing-driven microstructural modification, this approach uses a single thermal treatment to induce a finer and more uniformly distributed lamellar structure. The refined spacing is expected to enhance dislocation blockage (thus increasing strength) while preserving and possibly even improving the connectivity of the softer phase to facilitate dislocation mobility (thus enhancing ductility). This integrated mechanism directly addresses the inherent strength-ductility trade-off in eutectic HEAs and follows the cues provided by previous work.
